borders.before: the lecturer's self-introduction, the lecture series overview, and the stated learning objectives for this session
borders.after: the core definition of cancer as a genetic and evolutionary disease within a microenvironment
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is opening framing, whereas subtopic 2 begins substantive teaching on the nature and causes of cancer.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no earlier or later boundary that cleanly separates framing from content.
borders.caseForRemoving: Subtopic 1 introduces the course, while subtopic 2 delves into cancer biology.

borders.before: global epidemiological variations in cancer types and the interplay between genetic predisposition and environmental factors
borders.after: infectious pathogens (bacteria, helminths, fungi, viruses) and their mechanisms in driving carcinogenesis
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 7 transitions from general epidemiological patterns to a specific category of environmental causes: infectious agents.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 6 concludes the high-level epidemiology discussion, so subtopic 7 is the exact place where infectious agents are taken up.
borders.caseForRemoving: Pathogen-driven carcinogenesis is a focused mechanistic topic distinct from the broad overview of risk factors and epidemiology in subtopics 2-6.

borders.before: the detailed mechanism and epidemiological mapping of Burkitt lymphoma, EBV, and malaria co-factors
borders.after: chemical mutagens such as dietary aflatoxin, their reactive metabolite epoxides, and adduct formation
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 9 shifts the discussion from infectious pathogens to chemical and physical mutagens.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 8 finishes the case study on infectious agents (EBV/Burkitt lymphoma), making subtopic 9 the appropriate start for chemical/physical mutagens.
borders.caseForRemoving: Pathogens and chemical/physical mutagens involve distinct agents and mechanistic pathways.

borders.before: tissue-specific chemical activation, specifically aromatic amines in cigarette smoke causing bladder cancer
borders.after: non-mutagenic carcinogens, tumor promoters, and chronic inflammation starting with asbestos and mesothelioma
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 14 introduces the concept of tumor promotion and non-mutagenic chronic inflammation, as opposed to direct DNA damage mutagens.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 13 finishes the discussion of mutagens requiring metabolic activation, so subtopic 14 starts the promotion/inflammation section.
borders.caseForRemoving: Initiation (direct DNA mutagens) is functionally and conceptually distinct from promotion (microenvironmental and inflammatory drivers).

borders.before: a summary slide reviewing direct mutagens, xenobiotic metabolism, promoters, and host/tissue susceptibility
borders.after: methods to identify causes of cancer using high-throughput sequencing and mutational signatures
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 18 turns to the experimental and epidemiological methods used to determine carcinogenicity and identify mutagenic exposures.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 is a clear summary of the biological mechanisms discussed previously, so starting the methodologies section at subtopic 18 is correct.
borders.caseForRemoving: Mechanisms of carcinogenesis and methods of testing/detection are distinct pedagogical modules.

borders.before: in vitro mutagenicity testing using the Ames test and its limitations regarding tumor microenvironments
borders.after: final summary of lecture takeaways, risk-benefit evaluation of environmental exposures, and lecture conclusion
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 22 serves as the closing framing and concluding thoughts of the lecture.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 finishes the discussion on testing methods (the Ames test), making subtopic 22 the start of the closing.
borders.caseForRemoving: Closing framing and summary belong in a separate concluding topic.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2-3 define cancer and the balance between endogenous errors and inherited predispositions, while subtopics 4-6 focus on specific environmental mutagens and worldwide epidemiological data.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 through 6 form a single coherent introductory exploration into the general causes of cancer, contrasting intrinsic bad luck with environmental exposures and epidemiological observations.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 7 surveys multiple pathogens while subtopic 8 focuses entirely on Burkitt lymphoma.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopic 8 serves as the primary detailed case study directly illustrating the general pathogen concepts introduced in subtopic 7.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 9-10 introduce aflatoxin and UV light, whereas subtopics 11-13 dive deeply into polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, xenobiotic metabolism, and tissue-specific activation.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 9 through 13 all examine direct chemical and physical mutagens, their metabolic activation, and the formation of DNA adducts.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14-15 define tumor promoters (asbestos, TPA) and the two-stage carcinogenesis model, while subtopic 16 examines host life stage and developmental susceptibility.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 14 to 17 form an integrated discussion of non-mutagenic factors in carcinogenesis, encompassing microenvironmental promoters, inflammation, host developmental windows, and an overall summary.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 18 discusses mutational signatures from sequencing, whereas subtopics 19-21 cover epidemiological biobanks, animal models, and the Ames test.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18 through 21 all systematically address the lecture's core question of how scientists detect and prove carcinogenicity across genomic, epidemiological, in vivo, and in vitro methodologies.

topics.label: Lecture Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic introduces the lecturer, outlines the scope of the cancer lecture course, and presents the session's learning objectives.

topics.label: Cancer Etiology: Genetic Factors, Environmental Exposures, and Epidemiology
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore the definition of cancer and assess how endogenous biological processes, inherited predispositions, environmental exposures, and epidemiological patterns shape overall cancer risk.

topics.label: Infectious Pathogens in Cancer Development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infectious pathogens and co-factors contribute to oncogenesis, using the mechanism and epidemiology of Burkitt lymphoma as an in-depth case study.

topics.label: Chemical and Physical Mutagens and Mechanisms of DNA Damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine dietary toxins, radiation, and environmental chemicals, detailing the metabolic activation pathways and DNA adducts that induce mutagenic transitions.

topics.label: Tumor Promotion, Host Susceptibility, and Mechanisms of Carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics discuss non-mutagenic tumor promoters, chronic inflammation, and host developmental susceptibility windows, concluding with a comprehensive summary of carcinogenic mechanisms.

topics.label: Methods for Assessing Carcinogenicity and Mutational Signatures
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics review genomic mutational signatures, population epidemiology, in vivo animal bioassays, and the Ames test used to prove and evaluate carcinogenic agents.

topics.label: Conclusion and Risk-Benefit Considerations
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic concludes the lecture with a summary of environmental cancer factors and the everyday risk-benefit calculations involved in exposure to potential carcinogens.
